Five officers P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row facing north. R sits exactly in the middle. P sits to the immediate left of R. T does not sit at either end. Q does not sit next to P. Who sits at the extreme right end?
R is third and P second. T is not at an end, so T is fourth. Q cannot sit next to P, so Q is fifth and S is first. The order is S, P, R, T, Q.

X, Y and Z start a firm with ₹90,000, ₹1,20,000 and ₹1,50,000. X, the managing partner, gets an allowance of ₹4,000 a month. Z's share of the divisible profit is guaranteed to be at least ₹1,15,000, any shortfall being borne by Y alone. If the annual profit before X's allowance is ₹2,88,000, what does Y finally receive?
Allowance 48,000; divisible 2,40,000 in 3:4:5 gives 60,000 / 80,000 / 1,00,000. Z is 15,000 short, which Y pays: 80,000 − 15,000 = 65,000. GPSC CBRT, Sep 2026.
Two trains P and Q start at the same time from X and Y towards each other. After meeting, P takes 4 hours to reach Y and Q takes 9 hours to reach X. If P runs at 72 km/h, what is the distance XY?
Speeds are in the ratio √9 : √4 = 3 : 2, so Q = 48 km/h. They meet after √(4 × 9) = 6 h; P travels 6 + 4 = 10 h × 72 = 720 km. GPSC CBRT, Sep 2026.

Choose the word closest in meaning to “capricious”:
'Capricious' means given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour; fickle. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the grammatically incorrect conditional sentence:
If she would have studied, she would have passed.
'Would have' is not used in the if-clause: 'If she had studied'. GPSC-style practice item.
A comma introduces the direct speech, which is enclosed in quotation marks. GPSC-style practice item.
Change into direct speech: He asked her whether she would attend the meeting.
He said to her, “Will you attend the meeting?”
'Would' in reported speech returns to 'will'; question order is restored. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “He prided ____ on his punctuality.”
'Pride' is followed by a reflexive pronoun. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the part of speech of “after” in: “She left after the meeting had ended.”
It joins the clause 'the meeting had ended' to the main clause. GPSC-style practice item.
Select the correct indirect speech: He said to me, “You ought to see a doctor.”
He told me that I ought to see a doctor.
'Ought to' does not change; the pronoun 'you' becomes 'I'. GPSC-style practice item.
Select the correct indirect speech: “Hurrah! We have won the match,” said the boys.
The boys exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
Exclamations use 'exclaimed with joy that'; present perfect becomes past perfect. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “The flock of sheep ____ grazing on the hill.”
The head noun 'flock' is singular. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the one word for: “A person who walks in sleep”
A somnambulist is a sleepwalker. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The man ____ car was stolen lodged a complaint.”
Choose the correct form: “Every boy and every girl ____ been given a book.”
Subjects joined by 'and' but preceded by 'every' take a singular verb. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “He needs not go there today.”
As a modal, 'need' takes no -s: 'He need not go' (or 'does not need to go'). GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “I have two pens; one is blue and ____ is black.”
With two items, the remaining one is 'the other'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct question tag: “He used to live here, ____?”
'Used to' is past, so the tag uses 'did'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “magnanimous”:
'Magnanimous' means generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “Had the ambulance arrived earlier, the child ____.”
Inverted third conditional takes 'would have + past participle'. GPSC-style practice item.

Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph:
P. Hence, regular hand washing with soap is advised.
Q. Many infections spread through unwashed hands.
R. Water alone cannot remove all the germs.
S. Soap, however, breaks down their outer layer.
'However' contrasts with water; 'Hence' gives the conclusion. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct article: “Honesty is ____ best policy.”
Fixed proverb: 'the best policy'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “She insisted ____ paying the bill herself.”
Choose the correct tense: “I ____ to Paris twice so far.”
'So far' signals the present perfect. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “I look forward to meet you at the conference next week.”
'Look forward to' takes a gerund: 'to meeting'. GPSC-style practice item.
Complete the sentence: “Not until the report arrived ____ the matter.”
'Not until' + clause is followed by inversion in the main clause. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The clerk ordered pens, files and other office ____.”
'Stationery' means writing materials; 'stationary' means not moving. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct passive construction: “The clerk has not filed the application.”
The application has not been filed by the clerk.
Present perfect passive: has/have been + past participle. GPSC-style practice item.
Fill in the blank: “I would rather ____ at home than go out in this rain.”
'Would rather' takes the bare infinitive. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct inversion of: “If I had known about the problem, I would have helped you.”
Had I known about the problem, I would have helped you.
Third conditional inverts to 'Had + subject + past participle'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “If she had taken the medicine on time, she ____ better now.”
Mixed conditional: past condition, present result. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the one word for: “A person who is gradually recovering health after illness”
A convalescent is someone regaining health after sickness. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct question tag: “Open the door, ____?”
An imperative takes 'will you' as its tag. GPSC-style practice item.
Complete the sentence: “Not a single word ____ during the interview.”
Negative object phrase in front requires did + subject + base verb. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “Although he is rich, but he is not happy.”
'Although' and 'but' must not be used together. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct tense: “This time tomorrow, I ____ in a train to Mumbai.”
An action in progress at a future time takes the future continuous. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the meaning of the idiom “to bite the bullet”:
to face a painful situation with courage
'Bite the bullet' means to endure something unpleasant bravely. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “The accused was convicted ____ murder.”
'Convicted of' a crime. GPSC-style practice item.
Change into a simple sentence: “As soon as he saw the police, he ran away.”
On seeing the police, he ran away.
'As soon as' is expressed as 'On + -ing'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct transformation: “He is so weak that he cannot walk.”
He is too weak to walk.
'So ... that ... not' becomes 'too ... to'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “The patient was operated by Dr Rao yesterday.”
The patient was operated on by Dr Rao yesterday.
The prepositional verb 'operate on' keeps its preposition in the passive. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “gregarious”:
'Gregarious' means fond of company; 'reclusive' means avoiding company. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “It is no use ____ over spilt milk.”
'It is no use' is followed by a gerund. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “prudent”:
'Prudent' means careful and sensible; 'reckless' means heedless of danger. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the part of speech of “Neither” in: “Neither of the answers is correct.”
It stands for a noun and is followed by 'of'. GPSC-style practice item.
In the sentence “Wherever you go, I will follow you,” the clause “Wherever you go” is a:
'Wherever' shows place and modifies the verb 'follow'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct phrasal verb: “The patient's fever has not ____ even after three days.”
'Come down' means to decrease, as of a fever. GPSC-style practice item.
He was tired; however, he continued working.
A semicolon precedes the conjunctive adverb 'however', followed by a comma. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct modal: “She dare not ____ the Principal.”
The modal 'dare' is followed by the bare infinitive. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The red scarf was a perfect ____ to her white dress.”
'Complement' means something that completes; 'compliment' means praise. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “She was too tired that she could not walk.”
She was so tired that she could not walk.
'So ... that' expresses result; 'too' needs 'to + verb'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the one word for: “The study of the origin and history of words”
Etymology traces the origin and development of words. GPSC-style practice item.
Silent p: pneu-mo-nia. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct phrasal verb: “She ____ her mother in looks and manner.”
'Take after' means to resemble a parent or relative. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “diligent”:
'Diligent' means hardworking; 'indolent' means lazy. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct article: “____ more you practise, ____ better you become.”
'The ... the' with comparatives shows proportion. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “The train reaches Mumbai ____ the morning.”
'In' is used with parts of the day (morning, afternoon, evening). GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “She suggested ____ the meeting.”
'Suggest' takes a gerund, not an infinitive. GPSC-style practice item.
Complete the sentence: “Nowhere in the report ____ any mention of side effects.”
Negative adverbial in front: verb 'be' precedes 'there'. GPSC-style practice item.
In the sentence “The day when we met was memorable,” the clause “when we met” is a:
'When' here is a relative adverb qualifying the noun 'day'. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “The man, whom everyone thought was honest, cheated them.”
'Who' is the subject of 'was honest'; 'everyone thought' is parenthetical. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct modal: “He ____ have stolen the money; he was out of town that day.”
'Cannot have' + past participle expresses certainty that something did not happen. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “equivocal”:
'Equivocal' means open to more than one interpretation; ambiguous. GPSC-style practice item.
A compound modifier before a noun is hyphenated throughout. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “The poet and philosopher ____ dead.”
One article for both nouns means one person, so the verb is singular. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct article: “____ Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.”
Names of single mountains take no article. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the one word for: “A person who bears pain and hardship without showing feelings”
A stoic endures suffering with calm self-control. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct question tag: “There is hardly any water left, ____?”
'Hardly' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The population of Goa is smaller than ____ of Maharashtra.”
'That' replaces the singular noun 'population' to avoid repetition. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “recalcitrant”:
'Recalcitrant' means stubbornly resisting authority; obstinate. GPSC-style practice item.
Select the correct indirect speech: He said, “If I had known, I would have come.”
He said that if he had known, he would have come.
A third conditional is already in the past perfect and does not change. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The committee needs a ____ arbiter who has no stake in the outcome.”
'Disinterested' means impartial; 'uninterested' means bored. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “Let you and I settle this matter at once.”
Let you and me settle this matter at once.
'Let' takes the objective case and a bare infinitive. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “More than one candidate ____ failed the test.”
'More than one' takes a singular noun and verb. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct modal: “You ____ have bought the medicine; we already had it.”
'Needn't have' + past participle means an action done but unnecessary. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the meaning of the idiom “a swan song”:
a final performance or achievement before retirement
A swan song is a last appearance or work. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct passive construction: “I saw him enter the room.”
He was seen to enter the room by me.
A bare infinitive after a perception verb becomes a to-infinitive in the passive. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “Not only he is a good doctor but also a kind human being.”
'Not only' at the start requires inversion: 'Not only is he'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct phrasal verb: “The negotiators managed to ____ their differences before the deadline.”
'Iron out' means to settle problems or disagreements. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct passive construction: “Nobody can solve this problem.”
This problem cannot be solved by anyone.
Negative subject becomes 'cannot be + past participle ... by anyone'; avoid double negatives. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct conjunction: “Not until the results were announced ____ he realise his mistake.”
After 'Not until' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: 'did he realise'. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “Hardly had she entered the room than the lights went out.”
'Hardly' pairs with 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “He is the legal heir ____ a large fortune.”
'Heir to' a property or title. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “She is two years ____ than her cousin.”
'Than' follows 'older'; 'elder' is not used with 'than'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “She is entitled ____ a pension after retirement.”
Choose the correct passive construction: “The principal gave the students certificates.”
The students were given certificates by the principal.
With two objects, either can become the subject; the others misuse tense or roles. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “It is incumbent ____ every citizen to pay taxes.”
In the sentence “The fact that he had lied upset everyone,” the clause “that he had lied” is a:
The clause explains the noun 'fact' and acts as a noun in apposition. GPSC-style practice item.
You will need the following: a pen, a ruler and a pencil.
A colon introduces a list after a complete clause. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the meaning of the idiom “to carry coals to Newcastle”:
Newcastle was a coal-producing town, so supplying coal there is pointless. GPSC-style practice item.
Change into a complex sentence: “Work hard, or you will fail.”
If you do not work hard, you will fail.
'Or' (otherwise) becomes 'if ... not'; 'unless' already carries negation. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “She would have recovered sooner had she ____ the prescribed diet.”
'Had she + past participle' is the inverted third conditional. GPSC-style practice item.
Fill in the blank: “It is essential that he ____ present at the meeting.”
After 'it is essential that', the subjunctive (bare infinitive) is used. GPSC-style practice item.
Select the correct indirect speech: She said, “I used to play tennis.”
She said that she used to play tennis.
'Used to' does not backshift. GPSC-style practice item.
In the sentence “Hard as he tried, he could not lift the stone,” the clause “Hard as he tried” is a:
'Hard as he tried' means 'though he tried hard': concession. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “pragmatic”:
'Pragmatic' means dealing with things realistically; 'idealistic' is the opposite. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “Many a student ____ failed in this examination.”
'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct tense: “The professor, who ____ at this university since 1998, retires next month.”
'Since 1998' up to now requires the present perfect. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct passive form: “He wants someone to repair the clinic roof.”
He wants the clinic roof to be repaired.
The passive infinitive is 'to be + past participle'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “He is averse ____ taking risks.”
The only English word ending in -sede (with no other -cede form). GPSC-style practice item.

Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph:
P. Their report, however, was rejected by the board.
Q. A team of researchers spent two years collecting data.
R. They claimed their results proved the drug’s safety.
S. The sample size, the board felt, was too small.
Claim, then 'however' rejection, then the reason for it. GPSC-style practice item.
Which sentence contains an adjective clause?
I know the place where he lives.
In the key, 'where he lives' qualifies the noun 'place'; in the others the clause is a noun or adverb clause. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “munificent”:
'Munificent' means very generous; 'parsimonious' means extremely stingy. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “He failed the exam, ____ surprised nobody.”
'Which' refers to the whole preceding clause; 'that' cannot follow a comma. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “Walking down the corridor, the lights suddenly went off.”
As I was walking down the corridor, the lights suddenly went off.
The participial phrase dangles; only the clause with its own subject is correct. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “He is the man whom I think is responsible for the leak.”
He is the man who I think is responsible for the leak.
'Who' is the subject of 'is responsible'; 'I think' is parenthetical. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “She is one of those nurses who ____ always punctual.”
'Who' refers to the plural 'nurses', so the verb is plural. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct inversion of: “If he were to apologise, I would forgive him.”
Were he to apologise, I would forgive him.
'If ... were to' is inverted as 'Were + subject + to'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “Not only the students but also the teacher ____ responsible.”
The verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the teacher'. GPSC-style practice item.
Select the correct indirect speech: He will say, “I am busy.”
He will say that he is busy.
When the reporting verb is in the future tense, there is no backshift. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “extol”:
To extol is to praise highly; to denigrate is to belittle. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct passive construction: “Do not touch the wires.”
Let not the wires be touched.
Negative imperative passive: Let not + object + be + past participle. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “I remember ____ the letter yesterday; I posted it myself.”
'Remember' + gerund refers to a past act recalled. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct tense: “When we reached the cinema, the film ____ for ten minutes.”
Duration up to a past moment takes the past perfect continuous. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “Two-thirds of the work ____ completed.”
The verb agrees with the noun after 'of' (work, uncountable, singular). GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “Don’t forget ____ the register before you leave.”
'Forget' + infinitive refers to a duty not yet done. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct phrasal verb: “He tried to ____ his negligence as bad luck.”
'Pass off as' means to represent falsely as something else. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “He is the only one of the students who ____ passed.”
With 'the only one of', 'who' refers to 'one', so the verb is singular. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “perfunctory”:
'Perfunctory' means done with minimal effort; cursory. GPSC-style practice item.

Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a meaningful paragraph:
P. However, excessive use disturbs sleep and attention.
Q. Smartphones have made communication quick and convenient.
R. Doctors therefore advise limiting screen time at night.
S. Many people now depend on them for work and study.
Benefits first, 'However' introduces the drawback, 'therefore' the advice. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct phrasal verb: “The students were told to ____ before the examination.”
'Buckle down' means to start working seriously. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct question tag: “Everyone has submitted the form, ____?”
'Everyone' takes the plural pronoun 'they' in a tag. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “inexorable”:
'Inexorable' means impossible to stop or persuade; relentless. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the part of speech of “since” in: “She has not called since.”
It has no object or clause following, so it is an adverb meaning 'from then till now'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “All ____ glitters is not gold.”
After 'all', the relative pronoun 'that' is used. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “She is one of the best doctors who has served in this hospital.”
In 'one of the ... who', the relative pronoun refers to the plural 'doctors': 'have served'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The ____ surgeon was honoured with a national award.”
'Eminent' means distinguished; 'imminent' means about to happen. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “The reason is because he was ill.”
The reason is that he was ill.
'The reason is' is followed by a 'that' clause, not 'because'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct tense: “It is two years since he ____ smoking.”
'It is (time) since' is followed by the simple past. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “If I weren’t so busy these days, I ____ the conference last week.”
Mixed conditional: present state, past result. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “He is a such brilliant student that everyone admires him.”
The order is 'such a' + adjective + noun: 'such a brilliant student'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the meaning of the idiom “a Pyrrhic victory”:
a victory won at too great a cost
After King Pyrrhus, whose victory cost him most of his army. GPSC-style practice item.
Select the correct indirect speech: He said to me, “I am leaving now; will you join me?”
He told me that he was leaving then and asked if I would join him.
Mixed sentences use 'told' for the statement and 'asked if' for the question; 'now' becomes 'then'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “sycophant”:
A sycophant is a person who flatters the powerful for advantage. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The candidate ____ I believe is the best has been selected.”
'Who' is the subject of 'is'; 'I believe' is parenthetical. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “laconic”:
'Laconic' means using very few words; terse. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct article: “She has ____ little patience left, so she cannot wait.”
'Little' without 'a' means hardly any (negative); 'a little' would mean some. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “He is used to ____ up early.”
'Be used to' takes a gerund (to is a preposition). GPSC-style practice item.
Fill in the blank: “He is used to ____ up at five every morning.”
'Be used to' (accustomed to) takes a gerund. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the meaning of the idiom “Hobson's choice”:
an apparent choice where there is really no alternative
Named after Thomas Hobson: take what is offered or nothing. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct conjunction: “I would rather die ____ beg for mercy.”
Choose the correct word: “It is the best film ____ I have ever seen.”
After a superlative, 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “If it had not been for your help last year, I ____ in that examination.”
Third conditional for an unreal past situation. GPSC-style practice item.
In “The poor need our help,” the word “poor” functions as a:
After 'the', it names a class of people, so it works as a noun. GPSC-style practice item.
Fill in the blank: “Need I ____ the form again?”
The modal 'need' in a question takes the bare infinitive. GPSC-style practice item.
In the sentence “He behaved as if he owned the place,” the clause “as if he owned the place” is a:
'As if' introduces an adverb clause of manner. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct preposition: “The manager is liable ____ any loss to the company.”
'Liable for' a loss or damage. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct tense: “Since the clinic ____ in 2012, it has treated thousands of patients.”
After 'since' the clause naming the starting point takes the simple past. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the part of speech of “only” in: “He is the only candidate who passed.”
It modifies the noun 'candidate'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct version: “Many a patient have recovered after this treatment.”
Many a patient has recovered after this treatment.
'Many a' takes a singular noun and a singular verb. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “The doctor tried to ____ the anxious parents that the child was safe.”
'Assure' is used with a person; 'ensure' means to make certain. GPSC-style practice item.
Change into a complex sentence: “Having finished the work, he went home.”
After he had finished the work, he went home.
The participle phrase becomes a time clause with past perfect. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “The criteria for selection is very strict.”
'Criteria' is the plural of 'criterion': 'are'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “ebullient”:
'Ebullient' means cheerful and full of energy; 'dejected' means low in spirits. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the one word for: “A disease regularly found among people in a particular area”
An endemic disease is constantly present in a particular region or population. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word opposite in meaning to “sporadic”:
'Sporadic' means occurring at irregular intervals; 'constant' means continuous. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct inversion of: “The accident was so terrible that the road remained closed for hours.”
So terrible was the accident that the road remained closed for hours.
'So + adjective' in front position inverts the verb 'be' and the subject. GPSC-style practice item.
Change into direct speech: The patient asked the doctor whether he could go home that day.
The patient said to the doctor, “Can I go home today?”
'Could' returns to 'can', 'that day' returns to 'today', and the question order is restored. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “If he had listened to the doctor then, he ____ in hospital now.”
Mixed conditional: past condition, present result. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the error: “The secret must remain between you and I.”
A preposition takes the objective case: 'between you and me'. GPSC-style practice item.
Ends in -ible: irresistible. GPSC-style practice item.
The question mark stays inside the quotes and no comma follows it. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct form: “Neither he nor I ____ to blame.”
With 'neither...nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'I'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct passive form: “I don’t like people laughing at me.”
I don’t like being laughed at.
After 'like' the passive gerund is 'being + past participle'. GPSC-style practice item.
Identify the part of speech of “yet” in: “It was raining, yet we went out.”
It joins two clauses and shows contrast. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct word: “For ____ details, please contact the office.”
'Further' means additional; 'farther' refers to distance. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the correct conjunction: “It was not until midnight ____ the fever subsided.”
Cleft structure: 'It was not until ... that'. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the one word for: “Government by a small group of people”
Oligarchy is rule by a few persons. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the word closest in meaning to “ostensible”:
'Ostensible' means seeming or outwardly stated, though perhaps not real. GPSC-style practice item.
Choose the meaning of the idiom “to eat humble pie”:
to apologise humbly and admit one's error
The idiom means to accept humiliation after being proved wrong. GPSC-style practice item.
What comes next? BCD, EFG, HIJ, KLM, …
Each group starts 3 letters after the last one, with the same pattern inside: NOP. GPSC-style practice item.
Meera is 6th from the top and 18th from the bottom in a class. How many students are in the class?
What comes next? FGH, IJK, LMN, OPQ, …
Each group starts 3 letters after the last one, with the same pattern inside: RST. GPSC-style practice item.
In a group of 90 people, 42 like tea, 57 like coffee and 21 like both. How many like neither?
Ajay is the sister of Vijay. Vijay is the father of Suresh. How is Ajay related to Suresh?
Draw the family tree from the statements; the answer is Paternal aunt. GPSC-style practice item.
Neha is 20th from the top and 23rd from the bottom in a class. How many students are in the class?
What comes next? CDE, EFG, GHI, IJK, …
Each group starts 2 letters after the last one, with the same pattern inside: KLM. GPSC-style practice item.
In a group of 40 people, 19 like Hindi, 20 like English and 13 like both. How many like neither?
Statements: All cats are dogs. No dogs are pets. Conclusions: I. All pets are cats. II. Some pets are not cats.
Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I need not be true, II must be true. GPSC-style practice item.
Statements: Some roses are flowers. No flowers are plants. Conclusions: I. Some roses are plants. II. Some roses are not plants.
Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I need not be true, II must be true. GPSC-style practice item.
If KNIGHT is written as MPKIJV in a certain code, how is MEDICAL written in that code?
In the code each letter moves 2 places forward: MEDICAL → OGFKECN. GPSC-style practice item.
A shopkeeper marks an item 10% above cost and gives a 20% discount. What is the overall gain?
What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 1:25?
What comes next in the series? 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, …
Squares of 6, 7, 8, …. Next: 121. GPSC-style practice item.

The exam asks how a case is taken, which symptoms rank highest, how to read the response to the first remedy (Kent's 12 observations) and how dose and repetition are decided.
Hahnemann's rules for case taking (§§83 to 104)

Bring freedom from prejudice, sound senses, attention in observing and fidelity in tracing the picture (§83). Let the patient tell the story without interruption; then hear relatives and attendants (§84). Write in the patient's own words, each symptom on a separate line, leaving space to add details. Complete each symptom: where, what sensation, what makes it better or worse, what accompanies it. Never ask a question that suggests the answer or can be answered with a bare yes or no (§87). Add what the physician observes: appearance, behaviour, expression (§90). In chronic cases ask about small

Strange, rare and peculiar symptoms (§153). Mental generals, in Kent's order: will and emotions, then understanding, then memory. Physical generals: heat and cold, appetite, thirst, desires and aversions, sleep, sweat, sexual and menstrual function. Particulars: symptoms of one part, best when complete. Common symptoms of the disease diagnosis: lowest value. A general symptom is said of 'I' (I am chilly); a particular of a part (my knee aches). Boenninghausen's complete symptom = location + sensation + modality + concomitant. Guernsey's keynote = one prominent feature pointing to a remedy. Cau

Wait while improvement continues; repeating too soon spoils the cure. Repeat the same remedy when improvement has stopped and the same symptoms return. Antidote when symptoms take the wrong direction or a violent, needless aggravation occurs. Complementary remedy when the first has done all it can and the picture has shifted to a related remedy. Change the remedy only when the totality has clearly changed or the first prescription was wrong. An intercurrent remedy (often a nosode) is given when reaction is deficient or a miasm blocks progress.

Minimum dose (§§275 to 279): just enough for a gentle cure; too large a dose causes needless aggravation. The dose can hardly be too small (§279). Potency choice: greater susceptibility calls for higher potencies (Close). Mental and functional states and sensitive patients take higher potencies; advanced pathology, weak vitality and phlegmatic types take lower ones. Kent's series: 30, 200, 1M, 10M, 50M, CM, then DM and MM. Repetition: acute cases may need frequent doses. Hahnemann traced chronic disease to three infectious miasms (psora, syphilis and sycosis), with psora behind about seven-eighths of all chronic disease. Questions test how the theory developed and the features that separate the miasms.

Hahnemann saw chronic diseases treated homoeopathically keep returning in new forms. He studied the problem from about 1816, explained it to his pupils Stapf and Gross in 1827, and published The Chronic Diseases in 1828. Acute miasms run a course and end. Some, such as smallpox, measles and whooping cough, occur once in a lifetime and are fixed miasms . Kent divides an acute miasm into prodromal, progressive and declining periods. Chronic miasms never end on their own; the vital force cannot throw them off. Three stages of infection: the moment of infection; the whole organism becomes diseased

Homoeopathic Materia Medica is the record of the pathogenetic effects of drugs, found by proving on healthy people, together with toxicological data and clinical confirmations. Hahnemann's Materia Medica Pura (1811 to 1821, six volumes) is the first pure MM; Fragmenta de viribus (1805) recorded 27 drugs.

Drug provings on healthy people: the primary source (Organon §§105 to 145). Toxicology : accidental and intentional poisonings, which show the gross effects. Clinical observations : symptoms cured though never proved, marked as clinical. Animal experiments , for tissue changes only.

A modality is a condition that makes a symptom better (amel., >) or worse (agg., <): time, temperature, weather, position, motion, touch, eating, emotions. Nosodes are prepared from diseased tissue or the products of disease (discharges, cultures, morbid tissue). Hering introduced the idea; Burnett and Swan widened its use. Sarcodes are prepared from healthy animal tissues and secretions: Thyroidinum, Adrenalinum, Pituitrinum, Insulinum, Lac caninum. Imponderabilia are energies with no material substance: X-ray, Magnetis poli, Sol, Luna, Electricitas. A nosode is often used as an intercurrent remedy when the well-chosen remedy stops acting or a miasm blocks progress. Six sources of homoeopathic drugs: name the source, then the remedy Drug sources

Collect from the plant's natural habitat , wild where possible, healthy and free from disease. Collect in dry, clear weather , and use the plant fresh unless the monograph says dried. Potentisation (dynamisation) is the step-by-step dilution of a drug with succussion (vigorous shaking) for liquids or trituration (grinding) for solids. Hahnemann describes it in Organon §§269 to 271; §270 gives the LM method.

Used for insoluble drugs (metals, most minerals, many animal products): the drug is ground with sugar of milk . Each potency takes one hour : three rounds of 20 minutes, each of grinding and scraping. Insoluble drugs are triturated to the 3C (6X); then the 3C is dissolved in water, alcohol is added, and the potency goes on as a liquid ( conversion ).

Triturate the drug to the 3C . Dissolve 1 grain of the 3C in 500 drops of a water and alcohol mixture. Take 1 drop of this, add 100 drops of alcohol and give 100 succussions : this medicates poppy-seed-sized globules, 500 globules per drop . That is LM 1 (0/1). Dissolve 1 such globule in a drop of water, add 100 drops of alcohol, succuss 100 times: LM 2. And so on. The ratio is 1/100 × 1/500 = 1 : 50,000 per step. A pharmacopoeia is the official book of standards for drugs: identity, purity, strength and method of preparation. The Government of India set up the Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia Committee in 1962 , under Dr B. K. Sarkar . HPI Volume I was published in 1971 ; further volumes followed. Before it, Indian manufacturers followed the HPUS (USA) and the German pharmacopoeia. The HPI is listed in the Second Schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 , which makes its standards legally binding. Take the strongest mental and physical generals first, then the particulars that are peculiar. If no exact rubric exists, go to the larger general rubric: Kent's book is built to be used general first. There are two ways to count: numerical (how many rubrics a remedy covers) and qualitative (the sum of grades 3, 2 and 1). The totals guide the choice; they do not dictate it.

The eliminating rubric should be a characteristic general that is certain and of reasonable size. Never eliminate with a small particular rubric or a doubtful symptom: the true remedy may be missing only because the rubric is incomplete. Cascading elimination means each rubric eliminates for the next, all through the exercise.

Rubric conversion turns the patient's language into the repertory's language without changing the meaning. "I feel worse when people try to comfort me" becomes Mind – Consolation – aggravates . "I am scared to be alone at home" becomes Mind – Fear – alone, of being . "My headache is better when I press hard" becomes Head – Pain – pressure – amel . Use synonyms and cross-references, choose the rubric that matches the exact meaning, and when unsure take the broader rubric. Know where things sit: in Kent, thirst and food desires are in Stomach. Evaluation decides which symptoms lead the repertorisation. The most-tested idea: characteristic (strange, rare, peculiar) symptoms rank highest and common diagnostic symptoms rank lowest (Organon §153).

Mental generals , in their own order: Will (emotions: loves, hates, fears, desires) above Understanding (intellect: delusions, confusion) above Memory . Physical generals , the things the patient says of "I": thermal state, appetite, cravings and aversions, thirst, sleep and dreams, sexual sphere and menses, perspiration, time and weather modalities. Particulars , the things said of a part: peculiar particulars count; common particulars count least. (1) Oligo- or anovulation; (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, raised testosterone); (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (12 or more follicles of 2–9 mm, or ovarian volume over 10 mL). 10.1 Epidemiology, prevention and National Health Programmes

WHO definition of health (1948): "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely an absence of disease or infirmity". Spiritual health is a proposed fourth dimension. Epidemiological triad: agent, host and environment. For non-communicable diseases a web of causation (multiple factors) is used instead. Iceberg phenomenon: the visible tip is clinical cases; the submerged part is sub-clinical, undiagnosed and carrier cases. Hypertension, diabetes and malnutrition show a large hidden part. Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health states i

Prevention is matched to the stage of disease. Leavell and Clark gave five modes of intervention : health promotion, specific protection, early diagnosis and treatment, disability limitation, and rehabilitation. Each level of prevention acts at one stage of disease Natural history of disease runs left to right (Leavell and Clark; Park's PSM) No risk factors yet Risk factors present Disease, no symptoms Symptoms, disability pre-pathogenesis pathogenesis Primordial Stop risk factors from appearing e.g. healthy diet and exercise habits in children Primary 1. Health promotion 2. Specific protectio

Incidence: new cases in a period ÷ population at risk. It measures risk and is used for acute diseases. Prevalence: all existing cases (old + new) at a time ÷ total population. It is useful for chronic diseases and planning services. Prevalence = Incidence × Mean duration (P = I × D). Attack rate: an incidence rate used during an epidemic. Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts ÷ susceptible contacts; it measures infectiousness. Incubation period: time from infection to first symptom. Serial interval: gap between onset of primary and secondary cases. Herd immunity: a high proportion of i

Common-source, single exposure: cases rise and fall within one incubation period (e.g. food poisoning). Propagated (person to person): gradual rise, several waves (e.g. hepatitis A, measles). Endemic: constant presence in an area. Pandemic: spread over many countries. Sporadic: scattered, irregular cases.

Use the 2×2 table: TP, FP, FN, TN. Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN): ability to detect true cases (true positive rate). Specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP): ability to identify true non-cases. Positive predictive value = TP ÷ (TP + FP). It rises with prevalence . Negative predictive value = TN ÷ (TN + FN). A screening test should be sensitive; a confirmatory (diagnostic) test should be specific. Wilson and Jungner (WHO, 1968) gave the criteria for a screening programme.

Active immunity: from infection or vaccine; slow but long-lasting. Passive: ready-made antibodies (e.g. immunoglobulin, maternal antibodies); immediate but short. Cold chain: vaccines are kept at +2 to +8 °C in an ice-lined refrigerator (ILR) at the health facility. Most heat-sensitive vaccine: OPV. Freeze-sensitive vaccines (never freeze): Hepatitis B, pentavalent, DPT, Td, IPV. Shake test detects a frozen vaccine. Vaccine vial monitor (VVM): discard when the inner square matches or is darker than the outer circle. The full Universal Immunisation Programme schedule is in the Topic 8 doc.

In an epidemic, symptoms of several patients are pooled to form one picture, and the remedy matching it is the genus epidemicus (Organon §100–102). Hahnemann used Belladonna as a prophylactic in scarlet fever (1799). This is the classic historical example.

Safe water: free from pathogens and harmful chemicals, pleasant to drink, usable for domestic purposes. The daily need is about 150–200 litres per person in cities. Purification on a large scale: storage → filtration → chlorination. Slow sand filter: the vital layer (Schmutzdecke) of algae and bacteria on the sand surface does the work. Rapid sand filter: needs prior coagulation with alum; cleaned by back-washing. Chlorination: the free residual chlorine must be 0.5 mg/L after 1 hour of contact . India's "big four": common cobra, common krait, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper. Elapids (cobra, krait) are neurotoxic : ptosis, difficulty swallowing, respiratory paralysis. Krait bites at night and is often painless. Vipers are haemotoxic : local swelling and bleeding. The 20-minute whole blood clotting test shows non-clotting blood. First aid: reassure, immobilise the limb, no cutting or sucking, and transfer quickly for polyvalent anti-snake venom , which covers the big four. Implied consent: the patient's conduct shows agreement (e.g. coming to the clinic, holding out an arm). It covers only a general examination. Expressed consent: oral or written; written consent is needed for any procedure with risk. Informed consent: the patient is told the nature, risks, alternatives and consequences of refusal, in a language they understand. Age: a person aged 18 years or more can give valid consent (IPC 87). For a child under 12 or a person of unsound mind, the guardian consents (IPC 89). In an emergency , the doctor may act in good faith without consent (IPC 92). The BNS s

Civil negligence brings compensation; criminal negligence needs gross negligence or recklessness (IPC 304A, now BNS 106 ). Bolam test: a doctor is not negligent if a responsible body of fellow practitioners would have acted the same way. Jacob Mathew v. Professional secrecy: the doctor must not disclose what the patient tells them. Privileged communication: disclosure is justified when the law or the public interest requires it, e.g. notifiable diseases, a court order, a patient's infection endangering a spouse, or a danger to others (e.g. an epileptic bus driver). Records: keep in-patient records for at least 3 years ; keep medico-legal records until the case is closed . Inquest: an inquiry into an unnatural death. Police inquest is the commonest in India; magistrate inquest is mandatory for deaths in custody, dowry deaths within 7 years of marriage and exhumation. Medico-legal autopsy: ordered by the police or magistrate; relatives' consent is not needed. A clinical (academic) autopsy needs the relatives' consent. Dying declaration: a statement by a dying person about the cause of death; best recorded by a magistrate, but a doctor may record it if death is imminent. The doctor certifies that the person is conscious and of sound mind (compos mentis) . No oath
